title: Registration and device-enrollment data can be linked to a specific household and device set
description: During account registration and enrollment of cameras/sensors, the Home Hub receives identifiers such as account details, device serial numbers, network identifiers, and timing metadata. If these are stored or transmitted together, they can be linked to the same homeowner/household, enabling correlation of multiple devices and actions to one person or home.
assumptions: Assumes the registration/enrollment flow includes persistent account identifiers and device identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only provided threat-type applicability, not detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Enrollment messages may reveal identifying information about the homeowner
description: The registration flow likely contains personal data such as name, email, phone number, address, account username, or unique device identifiers. Exposure of this flow to unauthorized parties would allow identification of the homeowner and association with a specific smart-home deployment.
assumptions: Assumes personally identifying account data is submitted during registration or can be inferred from device/account identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Exact fields in the flow are not specified; applicability depends on what registration attributes are collected.

title: Homeowner may be unable to prove or dispute enrollment actions
description: If the Home Hub does not create trustworthy records of consent, registration steps, and device-enrollment events, the homeowner may later be unable to prove which cameras/sensors were enrolled, when enrollment occurred, or whether they authorized the action. This creates repudiation risk around privacy-relevant setup actions.
assumptions: Assumes enrollment actions have privacy significance and may later be disputed.
uncertainty_note: Threat depends on whether audit trails or confirmations are absent; not enough detail is given.

title: Registration and enrollment disclose sensitive home-setup details
description: This flow can disclose the existence, number, type, and placement context of cameras and sensors associated with a home. Such metadata reveals occupancy-monitoring capabilities, security posture, and aspects of household behavior, even beyond direct identifiers.
assumptions: Assumes enrollment includes device model/type and possibly room/location labels or similar setup metadata.
uncertainty_note: Location/placement details are inferred from common enrollment workflows and may not always be present.

title: Homeowner may be unaware of what personal and device data is collected during setup
description: If the Home Hub does not clearly inform the homeowner during registration and device enrollment, they may not understand what account data, device identifiers, telemetry, or household metadata are being collected and for what purposes. This undermines transparency during an especially privacy-sensitive onboarding step.
assumptions: Assumes limited notice or poor UX around setup disclosures.
uncertainty_note: Applies if transparency is insufficient; the flow description alone does not confirm this.

title: Collected setup data may be used for purposes beyond account creation and device onboarding
description: Data provided to register the account and enroll cameras/sensors could later be used for analytics, profiling, marketing, service improvement, law-enforcement sharing, or cross-device correlation without being necessary for the original onboarding purpose. This creates a use-detachment risk.
assumptions: Assumes secondary uses are technically possible and not strictly constrained.
uncertainty_note: Secondary use is a common privacy risk but is not evidenced directly in the flow description.

title: Registration and enrollment may collect more data than necessary or without valid consent/legal basis
description: The onboarding flow may request excessive personal details, collect unnecessary device metadata, or proceed without sufficiently specific consent/notice for enrolling cameras and sensors. Because these devices can capture highly sensitive household information, inadequate legal basis, invalid consent, or data minimization failures create non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes the system is subject to privacy obligations requiring lawful basis, transparency, and minimization.
uncertainty_note: Specific compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and implementation details; exact tree-node id is based on best judgement.

title: Temporary access code can reveal guest identity or visit pattern
description: The Home Hub receives a temporary access code from a guest. If the code is unique per guest or per visit, the value can identify or single out the guest and reveal that a specific guest is present at a specific time when processed or logged by the hub.
assumptions: Assumes temporary codes are unique or linkable to a guest, reservation, or visit window, and that the hub stores or forwards code-entry events.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include a specific Identifiability subtree citation.

title: Entered temporary access code may be disclosed to unauthorized parties
description: The guest submits a temporary access code to the Home Hub. If the code is transmitted, displayed, logged, or stored without adequate protection, an unauthorized party could learn the code and infer access rights or use it to unlock the door during its validity period.
assumptions: Assumes the code is sensitive authentication data and may be exposed via local interfaces, network transmission, diagnostics, or logs.
uncertainty_note: Threat is grounded in disclosure of sensitive authentication data on this flow; exact subtree node is best-judgement due to missing detailed threat-tree excerpt in context.

title: Guest may be unaware that entering the code shares personal data
description: By entering the temporary access code at the Home Hub, the guest may unknowingly provide personal data such as a unique identifier, presence at the property, and time of entry. If the interface does not clearly explain what is collected, logged, or shared, the guest may be unaware of this processing.
assumptions: Assumes the code entry event or associated metadata is logged, linked to a guest, or shared with other components or controllers.

title: Guest code entry may be processed without a valid legal basis or beyond stated purpose
description: The Home Hub processes the temporary access code and related metadata to unlock the door. If the system also logs, profiles, or reuses this event data for secondary purposes without an appropriate legal basis, transparency, or purpose limitation, the processing may be non-compliant.
assumptions: Assumes personal data is involved because the temporary code or event metadata can be linked to an identifiable guest or household visitor.
uncertainty_note: Exact non-compliance subtree node is best-judgement because no detailed Nc subtree was provided in the retrieved context.

title: Excessive retention and granularity of in-home event history
description: Writing detailed motion, door, and sensor events to the local event log can disclose intimate occupancy patterns, routines, sleep/absence periods, and household behavior if more event detail or retention is stored than is necessary for the hub's purpose. Even though the log is local, the datastore itself becomes a disclosure point for highly sensitive behavioral data.
assumptions: Assumes the logged events are linkable to a household or identifiable residents and that the log may retain timestamps and fine-grained event details beyond immediate operational need.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-judgment based on common LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimization structure; retrieved context confirms Dd applies to Process->DataStore but does not provide exact subtree numbering.

title: Local event log enables identification of residents through behavioral signatures
description: A persistent log of motion, door, and sensor events can allow identification or singling out of specific residents or visitors by their recurring temporal and spatial behavior patterns, even if direct identifiers are absent. The datastore therefore creates an identification risk from pseudonymous or seemingly innocuous event records.
assumptions: Assumes event records include timestamps, device/location context, or other attributes sufficient to distinguish household members or frequent visitors.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is approximate; applicability is based on identification from behavioral/event data stored in the datastore.

title: Event records are linkable into a comprehensive household activity profile
description: By writing all motion, door, and sensor events into one local datastore, the system enables linking separate observations over time into a unified activity history. This can reveal relationships between rooms, devices, routines, and occupants that would not be apparent from isolated events.
assumptions: Assumes the log aggregates multiple event sources under common timestamps, device identifiers, household identifiers, or other correlators.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is approximate; retrieved mapping supports Linkability on Process->DataStore/Datastore position, but not the precise subtree id.

title: Detailed sensor-event history enables inference of sensitive household facts
description: Stored motion, door, and sensor events can be analyzed to infer presence at home, daily routines, sleeping habits, vacations, religious practices, health conditions, caregiving patterns, or relationship status. The privacy risk arises from what can be derived from the logged data, not only from the raw events themselves.
assumptions: Assumes event frequency, timing, and sensor location/type provide enough signal for behavioral inference.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is approximate; threat applicability is strong for derivation from longitudinal event logs.

title: Logging household events without clear necessity or consent basis
description: Persistently writing in-home sensor events to a local log may violate data-minimization, purpose-limitation, retention, or consent/legitimate-basis requirements if users are not adequately informed or cannot control whether such events are stored. The flow creates a compliance risk when logging exceeds what is necessary for the stated function.
assumptions: Assumes the system is subject to privacy requirements and that event logging may be optional, excessive, or insufficiently disclosed to users.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is approximate; non-compliance depends on jurisdiction, product purpose, and whether suitable notice/controls/retention limits exist.

title: Upload metadata and account association can link clips to a specific household
description: When the Home Hub uploads recorded camera clips to cloud storage, identifiers in the upload channel or object metadata (account ID, device ID, IP address, timestamps, camera identifiers) can allow the cloud provider or anyone with access to the storage context to link multiple clips to the same home and infer occupancy patterns or routines.
assumptions: The upload includes persistent identifiers or metadata needed to organize clips in cloud storage.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include a specific linkability subtree citation.

title: Uploaded clips may reveal the identity of residents or visitors
description: Recorded camera clips are likely to contain faces, voices, interiors, and contextual details. Uploading them from the Home Hub to cloud storage exposes directly identifying and quasi-identifying information to the cloud environment, increasing the risk that individuals in the footage can be identified.
assumptions: The clips contain personal data such as images of people, voices, or uniquely identifying household context.
uncertainty_note: Specific identifiability subtree citation is approximate; the general threat clearly applies to this flow.

title: Cloud-stored video can disclose sensitive in-home activities
description: The uploaded clips may reveal behavior inside or around the home, including presence/absence, daily routines, relationships, health-related situations, religious practices, or other intimate activities. Sending these clips to cloud storage increases the number of parties and systems that could access or infer such information.
assumptions: The cameras capture private domestic spaces or activities and the cloud environment is accessible to provider personnel, processors, or attackers if compromised.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure subtree node is selected by best judgement; retrieved context did not provide the exact D subtree.

title: Cloud video storage may become a concentration point enabling broad personal-data disclosure
description: Centralizing recorded clips in Cloud Video Storage creates a large repository of sensitive household footage. If storage access controls, segregation, or encryption are weak, a single compromise or misuse event could disclose many clips and associated metadata at once.
assumptions: Multiple clips are retained in the datastore and could be accessed in bulk by insiders, attackers, or through misconfiguration.
uncertainty_note: The exact detectability/disclosure distinction can vary by LINDDUN Pro wording; this is modeled as data disclosure due to centralized storage exposure.

title: Residents or visitors may be unaware that clips are uploaded to the cloud
description: People captured by the home cameras may not understand that recordings are not only stored locally but also transmitted from the Home Hub to remote cloud storage. This lack of awareness undermines transparency about where personal data goes and who may access it.
assumptions: The system does not clearly notify all affected individuals about cloud upload behavior.
uncertainty_note: Specific unawareness subtree citation is approximate, but the transparency risk is genuine for this flow.

title: Uploaded clips may be retained longer than necessary in cloud storage
description: Once camera clips are uploaded to Cloud Video Storage, they may be kept indefinitely or for a default retention period that exceeds what is necessary for the stated purpose. This would violate the storage limitation principle for personal data.
assumptions: Retention periods are not strictly bounded, enforced, or configurable in line with purpose limitation.

title: Lack of upload evidence may prevent proving what footage was sent to the cloud
description: If the Home Hub does not create reliable, privacy-respecting audit records for clip uploads, users and operators may be unable to later demonstrate which clips were transmitted, when, and under whose authority. This can hinder accountability and dispute resolution around cloud storage of personal footage.
assumptions: Upload events are not strongly logged or logs are incomplete/tamperable.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation is less central than disclosure for this flow; included because upload accountability is a plausible privacy concern, but exact subtree citation is approximate.

title: Excessive disclosure in motion alert payload
description: The Home Hub may forward more personal data than necessary with the real-time motion alert to the backend, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, room/location labels, occupancy context, or raw sensor details. This can disclose household behavior patterns beyond what is strictly needed to notify the user.
assumptions: The alert concerns activity in a private home and therefore can reveal personal data about occupants' presence and routines. The backend may only need a minimal event indicator rather than full sensor context.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen as best judgement for explicit, avoidable disclosure/minimality on a process-to-process flow; retrieved context confirms Dd applicability but does not provide the exact subtree wording.

title: Backend can link motion alerts to a persistent household profile
description: Because the backend receives recurring real-time motion alerts from the Home Hub, it may be able to correlate events over time using stable hub, account, or household identifiers. This enables linking separate motion events into a detailed profile of occupancy patterns and daily routines.
assumptions: The backend can observe repeated alerts from the same hub/account over time and retains identifiers or metadata enabling correlation.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is best judgement; Process->Process mapping makes Linking applicable at the destination.

title: Motion alerts enable inference of occupants' habits and presence
description: Even if the payload contains only a motion event, the backend can infer sensitive information such as when residents are home, asleep, away, or following regular routines. Repeated alerts may also reveal work schedules, travel, or unusual activity.
assumptions: The backend stores or can analyze alert timing and frequency across multiple events.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is best judgement; inference risk is strongly supported by the nature of repeated motion-event telemetry.

title: Motion alert stream may identify a specific household or user
description: The backend may be able to identify the data subject behind the alert stream through hub identifiers, account bindings, network metadata, or installation context. A supposedly device-level event can therefore become attributable to a particular household or resident.
assumptions: The backend has access to account registration, device enrollment, or other metadata tying the hub to a person or address.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is best judgement; identifiability depends on backend enrollment/account design.

title: Unexpected secondary use of motion alerts may exceed user consent or expectations
description: Once motion alerts reach the backend, they may be processed for analytics, service improvement, security scoring, or other secondary purposes not expected by the household. This can create a non-compliance risk if the transfer and subsequent processing are not adequately justified, transparent, and limited.
assumptions: The service may retain or reuse alert data beyond immediate notification delivery.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is best judgement; compliance impact depends on stated purposes, notices, and legal basis.

title: Notification content may disclose personal activity or occupancy information
description: The backend sends a motion-detected push notification to the homeowner. If the notification content includes detailed event information (e.g., motion at home, room/camera/location, timestamp, image preview), it discloses personal data about the household's presence, behavior, and routines beyond what is strictly necessary to alert the user.
assumptions: Assumes the push notification contains event details or metadata beyond a minimal generic alert, and may traverse third-party push infrastructure or appear on a lock screen.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement for avoidable explicit disclosure/minimization; retrieved context confirms Dd applicability to Process->ExternalEntity flows but does not provide the exact subtree node.

title: Push notification metadata can reveal the homeowner's identity or household association
description: Even if the message body is brief, notification metadata such as device token linkage, account identifier, app instance, or household/site identifier can enable identification of the homeowner or association with a specific residence when the backend sends the alert.
assumptions: Assumes the push delivery mechanism or backend processing uses identifiers tied to a specific user, device, or home installation.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree node is inferred from general identifiability threats for data flows; context only establishes that Identifiability applies on this interaction type.

title: Repeated motion alerts may enable linkability of events and user behavior patterns
description: A sequence of motion-detected notifications sent from the backend to the same homeowner can be linked over time, allowing correlation of events, occupancy patterns, and daily routines. This may let observers or intermediaries infer when the home is active or unattended.
assumptions: Assumes notifications are observable in aggregate by the recipient device, platform provider, or another party with access to notification history/metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort; context confirms Linkability is applicable to Process->ExternalEntity flows but not the exact subtree.

title: Motion notifications may enable inference of sensitive household behavior
description: From the fact, timing, frequency, and context of motion-detected alerts, a recipient-side observer or intermediary may infer private information such as occupancy schedules, sleep patterns, travel, or unusual activity, even if the notification contains limited explicit content.
assumptions: Assumes timing/frequency of alerts are visible or retained and can be analyzed.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree node is inferred from detectability/inference-style threats on flows; not directly cited in retrieved context.

title: Notification delivery may occur without sufficiently informed or granular user consent
description: Sending motion-detected push notifications may process and disclose personal event data to the homeowner's device and possibly a push service provider. If users are not clearly informed about what data appears in notifications, lock-screen exposure, or third-party delivery involvement, consent and transparency may be insufficient.
assumptions: Assumes notification settings, content detail levels, or third-party push routing are not fully explained or separately controllable.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance is plausible here, but depends on jurisdiction, notice design, and consent model; exact subtree node is best-effort.

title: Analytics payload may remain linkable to individual users or devices
description: Although described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend's disclosure to the cloud analytics vendor may still include stable device, account, session, cohort, or event attributes that let the vendor link multiple reports to the same user, device, app instance, or household over time.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics are not fully anonymized and may contain persistent identifiers, quasi-identifiers, or fine-grained dimensions.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types by interaction but not detailed node ids.

title: Vendor may infer identities from aggregated analytics
description: The receiving analytics vendor may be able to identify or single out users, devices, or small groups by combining the received aggregates with its own datasets, IP/account context, timestamps, geography, or other auxiliary information.
assumptions: Assumes aggregates may be granular enough that re-identification or singling out is feasible when combined with external data.
uncertainty_note: Applies only if aggregation is weak or dimensions are sufficiently granular; node id is approximate.

title: Shared analytics may disclose sensitive behavior patterns
description: Even if direct identifiers are removed, device-usage analytics can reveal behavioral patterns such as app usage habits, activity times, feature adoption, location-related routines, or other sensitive inferences once processed by the vendor.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics include behavioral, temporal, or contextual dimensions from which sensitive facts can be inferred.
uncertainty_note: Depends on the actual fields and granularity of the analytics payload; node id is best-judgement.

title: Secondary analytics use may exceed user expectations
description: After receipt, the cloud analytics vendor may use the analytics for profiling, product improvement, benchmarking, model training, cross-customer insights, or other purposes beyond what users reasonably expect from the mobile app's stated functionality.
assumptions: Assumes contractual or technical controls do not strictly limit the vendor to a narrow processor role.
uncertainty_note: This is a common risk for third-party analytics sharing, but applicability depends on the vendor role and contractual restrictions; node id is approximate.

title: Transfer to analytics vendor may lack a valid privacy basis or exceed declared purpose
description: Sending device-usage analytics to an external analytics vendor may violate consent, purpose-limitation, data-minimization, transparency, cross-border transfer, or processor-controller obligations if the sharing is not properly disclosed and justified.
assumptions: Assumes personal data or pseudonymous data are involved and that compliance obligations apply to this transfer.
uncertainty_note: Compliance applicability depends on jurisdiction, the exact data shared, and whether the vendor acts as processor or independent controller; node id is approximate.

title: Backend retrieval of stored video can reveal viewing patterns and household activity
description: When the mobile app backend retrieves a stored video clip from cloud storage, the retrieval event and associated metadata (clip identifier, camera/home identifier, timestamps, requester/account context) can be observed or logged at the backend. This can enable linking a specific homeowner account to particular cameras, times, and occupancy/activity patterns inferred from the requested footage.
assumptions: The backend or surrounding infrastructure logs retrieval requests or can correlate request metadata with user/account identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types by interaction/position but not detailed node mappings for this exact case.

title: Retrieved video clip may expose identifying content beyond what is necessary
description: The backend receives the full stored video clip, which may contain directly or indirectly identifying personal data such as faces, voices, visitors, neighbors, interior details, routines, and precise timestamps. If the backend processes or retains more of this content than needed for playback, identifiability risk increases.
assumptions: The clip contains personal data and the backend has access to full-resolution content or rich metadata during retrieval.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; threat applicability is strong because video footage is inherently identifying.

title: Backend retrieval can disclose sensitive household information from video content
description: By retrieving the stored clip, the backend gains access to potentially sensitive information visible or inferable from the footage, such as presence at home, daily routines, visitors, children, health-related situations, religious symbols, or other intimate household details. Any unnecessary access, inspection, or secondary use at the backend constitutes information disclosure.
assumptions: Backend components, operators, logs, analytics, or downstream services can access the clip or extracted metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate; disclosure is grounded in backend receipt and possible processing of highly sensitive home-surveillance footage.

title: Retrieval and playback logs may allow deduction of homeowner behavior
description: Even if the backend does not inspect the clip content, repeated retrievals of specific clips, cameras, and times can allow deduction of behavior such as when the homeowner is away, what events they consider important, sleep/work schedules, or recurring visitors. Such inferences can arise from access patterns and metadata alone.
assumptions: The backend stores or can analyze retrieval metadata over time.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is best-judgement; deduction risk is based mainly on metadata and access-pattern analysis.

title: Backend may process or retain retrieved video in ways unexpected by the homeowner
description: A homeowner may expect the backend to act only as a transient conduit for playback, but the retrieval operation may involve caching, transcoding, analytics, debugging, or retention of the clip and metadata. If these backend-side uses are not transparent, users may be unaware of how their surveillance footage is handled.
assumptions: System behavior includes backend-side processing beyond immediate delivery, or this is not clearly communicated to users.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness depends on actual notices and architecture; included because backend retrieval commonly entails opaque intermediate processing.

title: Retrieval of stored video may exceed consented purpose or legal basis
description: If the backend retrieves and further processes stored video for purposes beyond homeowner-requested playback—such as service improvement, employee troubleshooting, analytics, model training, or extended retention—this may be incompatible with the original purpose or consent/legal basis for collecting the footage.
assumptions: There is potential for secondary processing or retention at the backend beyond strictly necessary playback delivery.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on actual governance and stated purposes; exact node id is approximate.
